newsitem.title: USA: Consumers, Internet firms join in access-fee dispute.
newsitem.headline: Consumers, Internet firms join in access-fee dispute.

text.p: If anything gets Internet users mad, it's the prospect of paying more for their online fix.

At least that's the consensus expressed in an avalanche of e-mail Internet users are sending the Federal Communications Commission about the dispute over Internet access fees. At issue is whether Internet service providers should pay local phone companies by the minute for use of the local telephone networks.
The FCC received more than 80,000 messages from consumers in one four-day period last week -- an unprecedented amount for a single subject over that time frame, according to an agency spokeswoman.

Mail, most of it from consumers siding with Internet service providers against access fees, continues to pour in at a rate of 30 messages a minute, and at one point, temporarily crashed the agency's e-mail computer server.

The FCC is considering levying access fees on Internet providers as part of more far-reaching telecommunications industry reform. The agency is expected to rule on the issue later this year after considering formal comments from phone companies, Internet providers, and other interested parties, including the Internet-using public.

Local phone companies favour the fees as payback for network upgrades they've made due to booming Internet use, upgrades they claim would otherwise have been unnecessary. Internet providers, on the other hand, maintain computer traffic poses no threat to local phone networks, and in fact, has proven to be a financial windfall.

Arthur Massei, a home-based small business owner, agrees that phone companies are benefitting, not hurting, from America's Internet use. Massei, one of thousands to write the FCC, said he pays $230 a month for four phone lines, a fax line, a cell phone and $16 a month for Internet access.
"My telephone and Internet costs are substantial, second only to rent," he said. "The current system is fair and should be kept in place. Please keep them from taking more of my money."
If forced to pay access fees, Internet service providers have said they would have no choice but to pass on those costs to their customers.

But even a nominal access fee of 1 cent per minute could double what his family pays for Internet access, said Ken Koike, another FCC letter writer. Koike's family of five -- himself, his wife and three sons ages 8 to 13 -- spends about two hours a day online.

"That averages to be 24 minutes per person a day, not at all an unreasonable time online," Koike said. "But at (one cent a minute), the extra access fee would be $36 a month .... and would make a huge difference in my family's monthly Internet access budget."
Internet user Wally Lorenc wouldn't mind paying a usage tax, if the money was earmarked for an interstate digital network, much like the interstate highway programme of the 1950s.

"Implementation of wideband network distribution, preferably via fiber optics and satellite delivery, is imperative to evolutionize communication technology's promise of tomorrow," Lorenc said. "Converging technologies demand (it)."

Phone companies have complained about computer traffic hurting the local phone networks since electronic bulletin boards first appeared in the early 1980s, said Gil Kloepfer, Jr., in his letter to the FCC.
"It's now 1997 and (local carriers) have not taken any steps to re-engineer their network to handle the increased use of circuit-switched data connections at reasonable cost," Kloepfer said.
His solution: local phone companies should establish inter- and intra-company digital networks and bill consumers by how much bandwidth they use.
"The lowest would be available at rates comparable to standard residential phone rates. Those customers who require greater amounts would be charged for more," he said.

"People cannot and will not understand all the underlying technology surrounding the phone system and Internet," Kloepfer said. "It is up to the public utility commissions and the FCC to assure that the public is being provided the best possible services for a fair and equitable price."

Phone companies and Internet providers are battling over access fees outside the United States as well. In Australia, local phone companies intend to charge telephone users by the minute for calls made to a modem, said Michael Oldman, a Melbourne, Australia, resident.
"If they do that, the Internet in Australia will fast become a toy for the rich and no one else," Oldman said.

The FCC recently extended the deadline for phone companies and Internet providers to submit formal comments on the access issue until March 24; comments are posted on the FCC's Web site at http://www.fcc.gov/isp.html.
Consumers can send informal comments to the FCC at isp(at)fcc.gov.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
